questions.stem: Which statement best describes an ecological niche?

options.text: The role of a species, including its resource use and interactions with biotic and abiotic factors
options.why: A niche connects the species to resources, conditions and other organisms that affect its growth, survival and reproduction.

options.text: The geographical place in which every member of a biological community lives
options.why: That describes a habitat or ecosystem location. A niche concerns one species’ role and interactions.

options.text: The trophic level occupied by a species in one particular food chain
options.why: Trophic level is one part of feeding relationships. A niche also includes other resources, conditions and interactions.

options.text: The full range of temperatures within which an individual remains alive
options.why: That describes tolerance of one abiotic variable. A niche covers far more than temperature.

questions.stem: Which organism could grow both where oxygen is present and where it is absent?

options.text: An obligate anaerobe
options.why: An obligate anaerobe can grow only without oxygen and can’t tolerate its presence.

options.text: A facultative anaerobe
options.why: A facultative anaerobe can grow in either the presence or absence of environmental oxygen.

options.text: An obligate aerobe
options.why: An obligate aerobe requires oxygen, so it can’t grow where oxygen is absent.

options.text: An obligate photosynthetic organism
options.why: Photosynthetic nutrition describes how carbon compounds are produced. It doesn’t identify tolerance of oxygen.

questions.stem: Which groups include organisms that use photosynthesis as their mode of nutrition?

options.text: Plants, animals and all fungi
options.why: Animals and fungi are heterotrophic. They don’t use photosynthesis as their mode of nutrition.

options.text: Plants, algae and several groups of prokaryotes
options.why: Photosynthetic nutrition occurs in plants and algae, as well as in several prokaryotic groups.

options.text: Animals, archaea and all bacteria
options.why: Animals are heterotrophic, and bacteria and archaea contain diverse nutritional types rather than one universal mode.

options.text: Fungi, algae and every group of protists
options.why: Fungi are heterotrophic, and protists have several nutritional modes. Photosynthesis isn’t shared by every protist.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the stages of holozoic nutrition in their correct order?

options.text: Ingestion, internal digestion, absorption, assimilation
options.why: Food enters the animal, is digested inside it, crosses into body fluids or cells, and is then used by its tissues.

options.text: Absorption, ingestion, assimilation, internal digestion
options.why: Food must be ingested and digested before its products can be absorbed and assimilated.

options.text: External digestion, absorption, ingestion, assimilation
options.why: External digestion followed by absorption describes saprotrophic nutrition. Holozoic digestion occurs after ingestion.

options.text: Ingestion, assimilation, internal digestion, absorption
options.why: Assimilation uses nutrients that have already been digested and absorbed, so it can’t occur before those stages.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a facultative mixotroph?

options.text: It can alter its use of autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition as conditions change
options.why: Facultative mixotrophs have flexibility in nutritional mode, while obligate mixotrophs require both modes.

options.text: It must use autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition together throughout its life
options.why: That describes obligate mixotrophy. The organism depends on both nutritional modes.

options.text: It changes between aerobic and anaerobic respiration when oxygen availability changes
options.why: That concerns facultative anaerobiosis, which is about oxygen tolerance rather than sources of organic carbon.

options.text: It consumes a varied diet containing both plant and animal material
options.why: That describes omnivory. Mixotrophy combines autotrophic and heterotrophic modes of nutrition.

questions.stem: How does a saprotrophic fungus obtain nutrients?

options.text: It ingests dead material and digests the material inside a specialized cavity
options.why: Ingestion followed by internal digestion is holozoic nutrition. Fungi don’t feed this way.

options.text: It secretes enzymes onto dead material and absorbs the soluble digestion products
options.why: Saprotrophic digestion is external. The resulting soluble substances can then cross into the organism.

options.text: It captures light and uses it to produce organic compounds from carbon dioxide
options.why: That describes photosynthetic nutrition. Fungi are heterotrophs and don’t photosynthesize.

options.text: It pierces living cells and withdraws nutrients without carrying out digestion
options.why: That resembles feeding by some parasites or herbivores. It doesn’t describe decomposition by a saprotroph.

questions.stem: Which statement about archaea matches the required B4.2 understanding?

options.text: Archaea form one domain and use varied ways of obtaining energy for ATP production
options.why: Archaea are one of the three domains, and their nutritional strategies are diverse.

options.text: Archaea form a kingdom of obligate anaerobes that all obtain energy in the same way
options.why: Archaea are a domain, and they aren’t restricted to one oxygen tolerance or one way of obtaining energy.

options.text: Archaea are photosynthetic bacteria that always release oxygen into their environment
options.why: Archaea aren’t bacteria, and the domain contains diverse nutritional strategies rather than one form of photosynthesis.

options.text: Archaea are eukaryotic decomposers that digest dead organic matter outside their cells
options.why: Archaea are prokaryotic organisms. External digestion of dead matter describes saprotrophic nutrition in some fungi and bacteria.

questions.stem: Which skull evidence best supports an inference that a hominid processed tough plant material?

options.text: Large grinding teeth, thick enamel and a robust jaw
options.why: Those features support repeated crushing and grinding under large forces, which fits tough or abrasive plant food.

options.text: Long pointed canines, cutting teeth and a lightly built jaw
options.why: Pointed cutting teeth suggest tearing rather than extensive grinding of tough plant material.

options.text: Small uniform teeth, thin enamel and reduced chewing surfaces
options.why: Those features provide little support for powerful, prolonged grinding of tough or abrasive foods.

options.text: Large eye sockets, a short face and a broad nasal opening
options.why: Those skull features don’t directly show how food was mechanically processed. Dentition and chewing structures provide stronger evidence.

questions.stem: A leaf-eating insect can survive a toxin in its food plant that kills related insects. Which adaptation best explains this?

options.text: A metabolic pathway that detoxifies the plant compound
options.why: Some herbivores can convert particular plant toxins into less harmful substances, allowing them to feed on defended plants.

options.text: A larger realized niche created by competitive exclusion
options.why: Competitive exclusion usually removes access to resources or separates competitors. It doesn’t detoxify a chemical.

options.text: A piercing mouthpart that prevents all chemicals entering
options.why: Piercing mouthparts obtain plant fluids, but they don’t guarantee that dissolved toxins will be excluded.

options.text: A fundamental niche that contains no biotic interactions
options.why: A fundamental niche describes potential based on adaptations and tolerance limits. It isn’t a mechanism for processing toxins.

questions.stem: Which pairing contains a behavioral predator adaptation and a physical prey adaptation?

options.text: Venom production by a predator and toxic secretion by its prey
options.why: Both are chemical adaptations. Neither example supplies the requested physical prey adaptation.

options.text: Ambush hunting by a predator and protective armor on its prey
options.why: Ambush is a behavior, while armor is a body structure that makes capture or consumption harder.

options.text: Sharp claws on a predator and group vigilance by its prey
options.why: This reverses the requested categories. Claws are physical, while group vigilance is behavioral.

options.text: Camouflage in a predator and rapid escape by its prey
options.why: Camouflage is physical and escape is behavioral, so the categories again run in the opposite order.

questions.stem: How does a liana reach strong light in a forest?

options.text: It grows from a tree branch and absorbs nutrients directly from the supporting tree
options.why: That wrongly treats the plant as a parasite. It also fails to describe a liana, which is rooted in the ground.

options.text: It remains on the forest floor and relies on tolerance of very low light
options.why: That describes the strategy of shade-tolerant shrubs and herbs rather than a climbing liana.

options.text: It stays rooted in the ground and climbs other plants for physical support
options.why: Climbing lets a liana place leaves in brighter light without building a massive self-supporting trunk.

options.text: It produces a tall self-supporting trunk that becomes part of the canopy
options.why: That describes a canopy tree. A liana uses another plant for support while remaining rooted in soil.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes fundamental and realized niches?

options.text: The fundamental niche is occupied during competition, whereas the realized niche exists only without competitors
options.why: The relationship is backwards. Competition helps determine the realized niche.

options.text: The fundamental niche concerns abiotic factors, whereas the realized niche concerns only food resources
options.why: Both concepts can involve resources and environmental conditions. The key distinction is potential versus actual under competition.

options.text: The fundamental niche is potential, whereas the realized niche is the actual extent under competition
options.why: Adaptations and tolerance limits set the potential niche, while competitors can restrict how much of it is occupied.

options.text: The fundamental niche belongs to a population, whereas the realized niche belongs to an ecosystem
options.why: Both terms describe the niche of a species. They don’t refer to different levels of biological organization.

questions.stem: Two species depend on the same limiting resource in the same place. Which outcome is consistent with competitive exclusion?

options.text: Both species keep identical niches indefinitely because competition increases the resource supply
options.why: Competition doesn’t create more of the limiting resource. Identical niches can’t be maintained indefinitely.

options.text: One species is eliminated locally, or both become restricted to different parts of their fundamental niches
options.why: Competitive exclusion can remove one competitor or produce narrower, more distinct realized niches.

options.text: Both species expand beyond their tolerance limits and occupy larger fundamental niches
options.why: Competition doesn’t immediately change physiological tolerance limits. It tends to restrict resource access and realized niches.

options.text: One species becomes a predator and gains energy by consuming the other species
options.why: Competition doesn’t turn a species into a predator. Competitors use the same limited resource.

questions.stem: Species A survives across a wide moisture range when grown alone but only in wet soil when Species B is present. What does the wet-soil range represent for Species A?

options.text: Its fundamental niche, because the range shows every moisture condition it can tolerate
options.why: The full range observed without Species B gives better evidence of the fundamental niche.

options.text: Its realized niche, because competition restricts where it actually occurs
options.why: Species A can tolerate more conditions, but competition with Species B limits its actual range to wet soil.

options.text: Its habitat, because moisture alone defines the complete place where it lives
options.why: Moisture is one abiotic variable, not a complete habitat. The question concerns potential and actual niche ranges.

options.text: Its trophic level, because soil moisture determines its position in a food chain
options.why: Trophic level describes feeding position. It doesn’t describe a species’ range along a moisture gradient.
